chunks: From him, from Safwan and Fudalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who pledged an item as collateral with his partner, and there was no clear evidence between them regarding it: The one holding the collateral claimed it was worth one thousand dirhams, while the owner of the collateral claimed it was worth one hundred. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The burden of proof is on the one holding the collateral who claims it is worth one thousand dirhams; if he has no proof, then the oath is upon the pledgor.'

And he said regarding a man who pledged an item as collateral with his partner: The one holding the collateral said, 'I took it as collateral from you for such and such,' while the other said, 'It is merely a deposit with you.' He said: 'The burden of proof is on the one holding the collateral that it is such and such; if he has no proof, then the oath is upon the one who owns the collateral.'

key_terms.رَاهِن: The pledgor / One who gives collateral

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on burden of proof and oaths in disputes over pledged collateral in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the procedural rules for resolving disputes over pledged items, specifically addressing conflicting claims regarding value or legal status (collateral vs. deposit). It establishes that the burden of proof (*al-bayyina*) lies with the party holding the item who asserts a specific valuation or nature, while the oath (*al-yamin*) falls on the owner if proof is lacking. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle of *al-bayyuna 'ala al-mudda'i* (proof is upon the claimant) applied to possession-based disputes.
